Deadlock: set of threads/processes each waiting on resource held by another in the set → none can proceed, ever. Classic case: T1 holds lock A, wants B; T2 holds B, wants A.

Requires all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion (resource non-shareable), hold-and-wait (hold one while requesting another), no preemption (can't forcibly take a resource), circular wait (cycle of waiters). Break any one → deadlock impossible.

Practical avoidance, most useful first:

- **Global lock ordering**: always acquire locks in the same fixed order (e.g. by address or ID) → no cycle. Standard fix.
- **Hold fewer locks**: one coarse lock, or shrink critical sections so no nested acquisition. Never call unknown code (callbacks, virtual methods) while holding a lock.
- **Acquire all-or-nothing**: `std::scoped_lock(a, b)` in C++, or `tryLock` with timeout → on failure release everything, back off with jitter, retry. Gotcha: without jitter, deadlock becomes livelock.
- **Avoid shared mutable state**: message passing, immutable data, lock-free/atomic structures, single-writer thread.
- **Detect and recover**: databases build wait-for graph, abort a victim transaction → app must retry on deadlock error. Also set lock/statement timeouts.

Not only mutexes: same shape appears with DB row locks (two transactions updating same rows in opposite order), bounded channels/queues (both sides blocked sending), thread pools (task waits on subtask queued to the same full pool), and `await`/`.Result` blocking on a single-threaded sync context.

Debugging: thread dump (`jstack`, `gdb thread apply all bt`, Go's SIGQUIT dump) shows who holds vs waits; ThreadSanitizer and `go vet`/race tools flag lock-order inversions before they fire.
